summary: The video side is built the way the board scans: H/V counters drive per-pixel fetch phases for the char, background and sprite layers. Sprites go through a two-stage per-line process (a scan of sprite RAM fills a 9-bit 'online' RAM during active display, then a first-write-wins line buffer is filled during flyback and cleared as it is read). None of this follows MAME's tilemap/pixmap/draw_sprites decomposition, though the adder constants match MAME because both copy the same board adders. The sound side does not model the discrete circuits. It is a 12-channel sample player whose start/stop/loop/no-retrigger rules and ship-volume handling match MAME's zaxxon_sound_a/b/c_w. Everything sits in one monolithic VHDL file with functional blocks rather than one module per chip, so the result is a hardware-leaning video core with a MAME-style sound substitute.

findings.signal: Raster-driven sprite line search into a 9-bit online RAM
findings.note: During active display (hcnt(8)=1) every sprite Y byte is added to VF plus a flip constant, and the sprite is copied into a 32x9 online RAM when the top three bits are 111; flag bit 8 marks valid entries. MAME instead inverts that test with a search loop (find_minimum_y) to get a start Y and then blits whole sprites.

findings.signal: Line buffer with first-write-wins and clear-on-read
findings.note: The buffer is written at twice the pixel rate during flyback only when the existing pixel is 000 (sp_buffer_ram_we), and is zeroed as it is read out during display. This is a hardware line-buffer mechanism, not MAME's reverse-order transpen overdraw.

findings.signal: Sprite fetch phases keyed to hcnt(3:0)
findings.note: Code, color, flags and X position are latched, and ROM addresses stepped, at fixed hcnt(3:0) phases 0000/0010/0100/0110/1000..., with ROM output latches strobed every 4 pixels. This is a scan-time pipeline tied to the pixel counter, not a per-sprite loop.

findings.signal: Background read straight from map ROM through adders, no pixmap
findings.note: The map ROM address comes from scroll + VF and HF + ~VF/2 + 0x40/0x38 adders. Tile code and color are latched when (~VF(3:1)+HF(2:0))=000 and graphics when it is 011, giving a skewed per-pixel fetch. MAME renders a 32x512 tilemap pixmap and then samples it with srcx/srcy arithmetic.

The flip-dependent constants (111 & ~flip & flip flip flip & 1 = F1/EF; 0x40/0x38) and the inverted scroll latch (not cpu_do) match MAME exactly. MAME's own code models the board's adders, so this match shows shared hardware math, not copying.

findings.signal: Time-sliced VRAM/sprite RAM access gated by hcnt(0)
findings.note: CPU writes to char and sprite RAM go through only when hcnt(0)=1, and the video side owns the address bus on the other phase (ch_ram_addr = VF(7:3)&HF(7:3), sp_ram_addr = 0&hcnt(7:1)). This is board-style bus sharing that MAME does not model.

findings.signal: Priority mux as palette-address override chain
findings.note: Each pixel's palette PROM address is chosen by a char-over-sprite-over-background override of the 8-bit address, built from latched color-select bits. MAME does this as successive layer draws into a bitmap.

findings.signal: Sample-player sound mirroring MAME's PPI handlers
findings.note: The board's discrete sound circuits are replaced by 12 WAV samples using MAME's file numbering (00..23.wav). Each sample's loop, one-shot or no-retrigger behavior (M-EXP and ALARM3 do not restart while playing) and the PA1/PA0 volume on the ship-noise samples copy MAME's start/stop/playing() logic.
Read/write decode masks (E000, E703, E707, E0FF) give the same mirrors as MAME's map. A correct core and a correct emulator must share this, so it counts neither way.

All of the board logic sits in one architecture, split into 'sprite machine', 'char machine' and 'background machine' process groups. These follow neither MAME function names nor physical chips/PALs, and signal names (hcnt/vcnt, hflip/vflip) are generic rather than schematic net names.
Opcode/data decryption uses a 128-entry table indexed by address and data bits. This is the encryption chip's function, needed by both sides, so it says nothing about provenance.
